messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The crash happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late autumn. Kwame was on the floor of the exchange, screaming into a headset, when he missed the call from his sister. By the time he checked his voicemail, his mother had already been gone for two hours—a sudden, massive stroke that took her while she was standing at the kitchen sink. He had not been there. He had not answered the phone. In the weeks that followed, that single missed connection became the center around which everything else collapsed.

What he could remember of that day came in fragments—the color of the stock ticker when he finally looked up, the way his boss’s mouth moved without sound, the cold tile of the bathroom floor where he had sat after listening to the voicemail. But the rest was missing. When he tried to deliberately call up the memory of his mother’s face from that morning, or the sound of her voice the last time they spoke, there was only a blank, static wall. He could not hold the whole picture in his mind, and that incompleteness terrified him. He began to go over and over why this had happened to him—why he had been working, why he had not felt something coming, why he had not been a better son. The rumination was relentless, a loop that played every night in the dark of his empty apartment, and it made the fragments that did surface feel even more jagged and accusing.

The fragments themselves were sudden and without warning. A flash of his mother’s hand on the phone receiver. The smell of her kitchen. And then, without any transition, he would be back in that bathroom, heart pounding, certain for a moment that he was still there, that the loss was happening again in real time. These flashbacks brought with them a wave of raw, unmanageable emotion—guilt so sharp it felt like a physical wound, and a pervasive, low-grade shame that he had somehow failed the most basic duty of a son. The threat he felt was not from the outside world but from inside his own mind: the fear that he would be ambushed again by a memory, that his own brain was a trap. In response, he tried hard not to think about the trauma at all. He suppressed every thought that drifted toward his mother, every image of her face, every echo of her voice. He stopped visiting the neighborhood where she had lived. He threw out the voicemail without listening to it again. He avoided grief reminders the way a man might avoid a minefield, stepping carefully around any object or place or conversation that might trigger the pain.

But the suppression had a cost. The more he pushed the memory away, the more fragmented and strange it became when it returned—a jagged shard of sound or image that made no sense and carried no context, which in turn made the flashbacks more frightening and the guilt more intense. He began to take risks at work that he never would have considered before: leveraged positions that made his junior traders blanch, trades placed on instinct rather than analysis. It was not that he wanted to harm himself, exactly. It was that the danger felt familiar, almost grounding. The rush of a risky trade was the only thing that drowned out the rumination for a few hours, and the fear of losing money was simpler than the fear of his own memories. His colleagues noticed. His manager pulled him aside twice. Kwame dismissed the concerns with a wave of his hand, but he knew, somewhere beneath the surface, that he was steering into the storm.

He is sitting now in a clinician’s office for the first time, a man of sixty-two who has built a career on precision and control, reduced to describing a mind that feels like a broken radio. He is most afraid of one thing: that if he stops suppressing the memories, if he lets himself think about his mother deliberately, the guilt will drown him. But the fragments keep coming, and the risky trades are getting riskier, and he has begun to wonder, in the quiet moments before sleep, whether the crash he is steering toward is one he can walk away from.
